extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers; journalists and newspaper editors
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and editorial practice for wartime newspaper articles (Associated Press-style dispatches and related press policy commentary). Covers field reporting, publication constraints, and press freedom advocacy during World War II.

rubrics_metrics.name: News freedom at source
rubrics_metrics.description: "news at its source shall be freely available to all everywhere" (Kent Cooper: correspondents should have direct and equal access to the news of all governments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No country should give preferential transmission facilities to its own press as against the press of any other country; correspondents and press associations everywhere should have direct and equal access to government news and equal facilities to transmit it to their countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: No preferential transmission facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: "no country shall give preferential transmission facilities to its own press as against the press of any other country."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telecommunication and transmission infrastructure should be made equally available so that domestic papers are not favored in receiving and sending news; this is part of ensuring global news freedom and fair access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press leadership for international news freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: The American press should assume "militant leadership to obtain international news freedom at the next peace conference."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and publishers are urged to take an active, assertive role in pushing for international guarantees of press freedom in postwar policy discussions and peace negotiations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to governmental suppression/control of the press
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppression and control of the press by governments are described as a primary cause of wars; a free press is a central demand for postwar settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial policy and advocacy should emphasize resisting censorship and governmental controls, arguing for freedom of information as both a moral and practical deterrent to conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security clearance before publishing sensitive wartime details
rubrics_metrics.description: Some wartime details (e.g., full story of raids) should not be released until security aspects are cleared by the War or Navy Departments (Elmer Davis on Tokio raid coverage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters and editors must coordinate with military authorities and withhold publication of operationally sensitive information until officially cleared to avoid jeopardizing operations or personnel; balance public information with security needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and inter-agency verification of government releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Government releases (e.g., OWI rubber report) must be accurate and, when disputed, should be corrected if a responsible official demonstrates error (Jeffers–Davis exchange).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists and government communicators should ensure facts are certified by the responsible office before publication; if inaccuracies are identified, they should be promptly corrected and reconciled among agencies to maintain public confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of monopoly in news-gathering/ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Founders of the AP asserted they 'in no sense sought a monopoly' and opposed monopoly as a menace to national interest; mutual ownership was preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations should promote competition and mutualized, cooperative ownership structures rather than concentrating control in monopolies, to preserve independent reporting and internal editorial vigilance.
